subject: Is there way to determine abundances differences between three treatments?

messages.author: aa0ac95c68ba2dcc
messages.subject: Is there way to determine abundances differences between three treatments?
parts:
Hello,

I apologize if this is a simple answer, but so far I am stumped. For my study I have three treatments (Control, HC, and SI) in a random block design where I conducted point counts 5 times in both 2016 and 2017. I used gdistsamp (stacking the data to account for multiple years) to model the effect of treatment on species abundances, and tested the goodness of fit for each model with 100 simulations. 

Now that I have predicted abundances for each treatment is there a way to compare the abundances between all three treatments? Control is the intercept for my models, so I can see if there is a difference between Control and HC and then between Control and SI, but I haven't found any way to compare HC and SI directly. I have plotted my predicted values with confidence intervals, but I'm not sure there is a solid way to determine if they are significantly different from one another. Is there something simple I am missing? 

Here is an example of my model and predicted abundances from one species if that helps. 

> coye.trt.obs2

gdistsamp(lambdaformula = ~Treatment, phiformula = ~1, pformula = ~Obs, 
    data = coyeframe, keyfun = "hazard", output = "abund", mixture = "NB")

> coye.pred2 <- predict(coye.trt.obs2, type = "lambda", newdata = trt, appendData=T, interval="confidence")

Thanks!

messages.author: 02d195331194f5bd
messages.subject: Re: Is there way to determine abundances differences between three treatments?
parts:
Here's a partial answer to get you started. This gives a good overview of what's happening with categorical predictors in linear models, but it sounds like you already understand most (or all) of that. What you want is contrasts. Here's an overview of contrasts in R. Unfortunately, I'm not really going to answer your question because I'm not sure if/how you would implement contrasts in unmarked. 

One work-around is to set either HC or SI as the first factor level (so that it's treated as the intercept) and run a 2nd model. Another work-around is to run a model without an intercept. This would increase the number of parameters in the model by 1. Instead of estimating 2 effects (difference between level 1 and level 2; difference between level 1 and level 3), the model would estimate 3 effects (mean of control, mean of HC, mean of SI). You could then see whether or not the confidence intervals for the mean of each of the treatments overlap.
